## About these materials

::: {.callout-warning collapse="true"}
## Citation statement
Please cite these materials as: Schönbrodt, F., & Gupta, R. (2026). *Introduction to open research data: Why should we share data?* [Slides]. [LMU Open Science Center](https://www.osc.lmu.de/). [https://lmu-osc.github.io/teaching-material-for-novices/open-materials/open-data](https://lmu-osc.github.io/teaching-material-for-novices/open-materials/open-data)
:::

**Welcome!** These slides are intended to provide learners with an **introduction to open research data**. They cover **five reasons** to share data, from verifiability and self-correction to funder and journal requirements, and show how rarely data "available upon request" is actually shared. Learners then explore **what counts as research data** in their field, how to make data **"FAIR enough"**, and the **three fields of tension** that come with data sharing: privacy, the right of first usage (and the question of co-authorship), and protecting original authors. The session closes with how research assessment is starting to **reward open data**.

### Who are these materials for?

- **Educators** in higher education with or without familiarity with open research planning to **teach open research** to **novices**
- **Self-learners** with no or limited familiarity with open research planning to **develop and build** up on their open research skills

### Learning objectives

At the end of this session, you or your learners will be able to ...

- **Explain** why open data matters for verifiability, efficiency, public value, data persistence, and funder and journal requirements
- **Identify** what counts as research data in your own field
- **Apply** a "FAIR enough" approach to sharing your own data
- **Weigh** openness against privacy, the right of first usage, and the protection of original authors
- **Recognize** how research assessment is starting to value open data
